subject: Modern History
sub_topic: British trade policy — one-way free trade

concepts.name: Definition and Mechanics of One-Way Free Trade
key_dimensions: Distinction between genuine free trade (reciprocal) vs. one-way free trade (asymmetric) imposed on India
How British manufacturers enjoyed open access to Indian markets while Indian exports faced tariff barriers in Britain
Role of the East India Company's monopoly transitioning to Crown-administered asymmetric trade
Comparison with mercantilist policies of earlier European powers — why Britain's approach was structurally different

concepts.name: Dismantling of Indian Protective Tariffs (1813–1882)
key_dimensions: Charter Act of 1813 — ending EIC monopoly and opening India to British goods under low or zero tariffs
Successive tariff reductions forced on India: 1859, 1875, and the controversial abolition of import duties on cotton goods in 1882
Contrast: India had no sovereign power to set tariffs unlike self-governing dominions like Canada or Australia
UPSC trap — students confuse 'free trade' imposed on India with India voluntarily adopting free trade principles

concepts.name: Lancashire Cotton Interest and India's Textile Industry
key_dimensions: How British cotton mill owners (Lancashire lobby) directly influenced India's tariff policy through Parliament
Excise duty imposed on Indian-manufactured cotton goods (1894) to neutralize Indian mills' competitiveness — a double blow
Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt's critique of excise duties as proof of deliberate deindustrialization policy
UPSC trap — the excise duty was NOT a revenue measure but a protective measure for British mills; candidates often misclassify it

concepts.name: Deindustrialization of India — Causes and Extent
key_dimensions: Destruction of traditional handicraft industries (textiles, metal work, shipbuilding) due to flood of cheap British machine-made goods
Debate: Was deindustrialization caused by free trade policy alone or also by technology gap and loss of royal patronage?
Regional variation — Bengal's muslin industry vs. Bombay's surviving cotton mills; not uniform across India
UPSC trap — deindustrialization is often conflated with mere 'decline of handicrafts'; the structural unemployment dimension is critical

concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory — Dadabhai Naoroji's Framework
key_dimensions: Core argument in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901): India's wealth drained through trade surplus not returned as investment
Three channels of drain: Home Charges, profit repatriation by British firms, and salaries/pensions of British officials
How one-way free trade enabled the drain — India exported raw materials cheaply, imported manufactures expensively
UPSC trap — candidates must distinguish 'drain theory' (Naoroji) from 'surplus theory' and 'de-industrialization thesis' (R.C. Dutt) — they are related but distinct arguments

concepts.name: R.C. Dutt's Economic History Thesis and Policy Critique
key_dimensions: R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' (1902–1904): systematic documentation of tariff policy's destructive impact
Dutt's argument that British land revenue and trade policy together caused Indian poverty — holistic critique
His specific criticism of post-1813 tariff regime and 1882 cotton tariff abolition as policy decisions, not market outcomes
Distinction between Dutt's reformist approach (wanted policy change within empire) vs. later nationalist demand for complete economic independence

concepts.name: Home Charges and Their Connection to Trade Policy
key_dimensions: Home Charges: annual payment by Indian government to Britain for 'services' — civil/military pensions, debt interest, India Office expenses
How Home Charges created a structural trade surplus for India that was never reinvested — the mechanism of drain
Magnitude: estimated ₹30–35 crore annually in late 19th century — roughly one-third of government revenue
UPSC trap — Home Charges are sometimes presented as India's 'debt repayment' but critics argue these were illegitimate extractions; candidates must present both sides

concepts.name: Tariff Autonomy — India's Lack Thereof vs. British Dominions
key_dimensions: Self-governing dominions (Canada 1879, Australia 1901) could impose protective tariffs; India could not despite being larger economy
India as a 'dependent colony' vs. 'settler colony' distinction in terms of economic sovereignty
Fiscal Commission of 1921 and the eventual (partial) grant of tariff autonomy — context and limitations
UPSC angle — why the Government of India Act 1919 did NOT grant full tariff autonomy even during Montagu-Chelmsford reforms

concepts.name: Impact on Indian Shipbuilding Industry
key_dimensions: India had a thriving shipbuilding industry (Bombay, Surat, Masulipatnam) before British dominance
British Navigation Acts (applied to India post-1813) and preferential freight rates destroyed Indian shipping competitiveness
Unlike textiles, shipbuilding decline is less discussed — a high-yield area for UPSC mains differentiation
Contrast with Japan: Japan protected its shipbuilding; India could not — illustration of tariff autonomy's importance

concepts.name: Raw Material Export Orientation of Indian Economy
key_dimensions: British trade policy deliberately restructured India as supplier of raw materials: cotton, jute, indigo, opium, wheat
Railway network built primarily to facilitate raw material extraction to ports, not internal industrialization
Terms of trade deterioration: prices of primary commodities fell relative to manufactures in late 19th century — India doubly hurt
UPSC trap — railways are often praised as modernizing force; candidates must also present the 'extraction infrastructure' critique

concepts.name: Opium Trade and India's Forced Role in British Commerce
key_dimensions: India forced to produce and export opium to China to balance Britain's trade deficit with China — India had no say
Revenue from opium (Bengal Presidency) was a significant portion of Indian budget — dependency created deliberately
Moral critique by Indian nationalists: India made complicit in drug trade for British commercial benefit
UPSC angle — connects trade policy with diplomatic history (Opium Wars) and ethical dimensions of colonial economy

concepts.name: Indigo Cultivation and Plantation Economy as Trade Policy Instrument
key_dimensions: Indigo System in Bengal: European planters forced peasants to grow indigo for British textile dye industry under exploitative contracts
Nil Darpan (1858–59) and Indigo Commission (1860) — responses to Indigo Revolt revealing policy dimensions
Decline of indigo after synthetic dyes (1890s) — how dependent economies suffer when imperial needs change
Distinction: Indigo system was a private-colonial nexus, not purely state policy — nuance important for UPSC

concepts.name: British Capital Investment in India — Character and Consequences
key_dimensions: British investment concentrated in railways, plantations, export trade — NOT in building Indian manufacturing capacity
Profit repatriation meant investment did not generate retained surplus for Indian development
Contrast with German/American foreign investment which often involved technology transfer — British investment was extractive
UPSC trap — British investment is sometimes cited as a 'benefit' of colonial rule; candidates must analyze its structural character

concepts.name: Impact on Indian Artisans and Weavers — Social Consequences
key_dimensions: Occupational displacement of weavers, spinners, dyers — movement to agricultural sector increased pressure on land
Bengal famine connections: loss of supplementary weaving income reduced resilience of peasant households
Gender dimension: women spinners particularly affected as spinning (charkha) was women's work — foreshadows Gandhi's emphasis on khadi
UPSC angle — connects economic history with social history and Gandhi's later economic philosophy

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement as Economic Response to One-Way Free Trade
key_dimensions: 1905 Swadeshi Movement: boycott of British goods as direct political-economic response to colonial trade policy
Economic nationalism — Tilak, Aurobindo's emphasis on building Indian industry vs. Gokhale's moderate reform approach
Swadeshi as precursor to Gandhi's constructive programme — continuity and evolution of anti-colonial economic thought
UPSC trap — Swadeshi 1905 was triggered by Partition of Bengal (political cause) but had deep economic roots in trade grievances — candidates must connect both

concepts.name: Fiscal Policy of Colonial India — Revenue Priorities vs. Development
key_dimensions: Indian revenues used to fund British military campaigns (Afghanistan, Burma, China) — 'financial drain via military'
Low expenditure on education, health, industrialization vs. high expenditure on army and British administration
Famine relief deliberately kept minimal — Famine Codes (1883) acknowledged famines but prioritized fiscal orthodoxy
UPSC angle — connects trade policy with fiscal policy; Amartya Sen's entitlement theory of famines connects to trade and employment loss

concepts.name: Indian National Congress's Early Economic Critique (1885–1905)
key_dimensions: Early INC resolutions specifically targeting trade and tariff policy — often overlooked by candidates who focus on political demands
Dadabhai Naoroji as Congress President (1886, 1906) — institutionalization of economic critique within nationalist politics
Distinction between 'Moderate' economic demands (tariff reform, Indianization of services) vs. later radical demands
UPSC trap — early Congress is often dismissed as 'loyalist'; its systematic economic critique was substantive and data-driven

concepts.name: Comparative Perspective — Japan vs. India: Role of Trade Policy
key_dimensions: Japan (Meiji Restoration 1868): retained tariff autonomy, protected infant industries, achieved industrialization by 1900
India: no tariff autonomy, subjected to one-way free trade, remained deindustrialized — same time period, opposite outcomes
This comparison used by nationalists (Gokhale, Naoroji) to argue India's poverty was policy-caused, not civilizational
UPSC mains value — comparative answer demonstrating counterfactual reasoning scores higher than descriptive answers

concepts.name: Post-WWI Partial Shift in British Trade Policy Toward India
key_dimensions: WWI revealed India's lack of industrial base as strategic vulnerability — some protection reluctantly granted post-war
Indian Fiscal Commission (1921) and limited protective tariffs for iron/steel, cotton — India's first taste of tariff autonomy
Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO, 1907) growth accelerated by wartime demand and post-war protection — case study
UPSC trap — candidates must note this shift was partial and reluctant, not a genuine reversal of colonial trade philosophy; full tariff autonomy only after independence

concepts.name: Nationalist Economic Thought — Alternative Development Vision
key_dimensions: G.V. Joshi, M.G. Ranade's 'constructive nationalism': advocated state-led industrialization, protective tariffs, technical education
Ranade's 'Essays on Indian Economics' (1898) — systematic argument for protective tariff as development tool
Gandhi's economic model: village self-sufficiency and khadi as rejection of export-oriented colonial economy
Nehru's industrial policy (post-1947) directly informed by colonial trade policy failures — historical continuity into policy
